The Pentateuch, from the Greek word for five scrolls, is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible—Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy—collectively known in Jewish tradition as the Torah or Law. These texts form the foundational scriptures of Judaism and are central to Jewish religious practice, law, and identity, and Christian traditions include these same five books as the opening of the Old Testament, making the Pentateuch one of the most influential religious texts in Western civilization.

Genesis contains the creation narrative and the stories of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and the account of humanity's origins and the covenant with Abraham. Exodus tells of the liberation of the Israelites from Egyptian slavery under Moses, the Sinai covenant, and the giving of the Ten Commandments. Leviticus contains detailed laws of priests, sacrifice, purity, and holiness, and is the most legal and ritual-focused of the five books. Numbers records the wilderness wanderings of the Israelites for forty years, census-taking, and laws governing the community and priesthood. Deuteronomy contains Moses' farewell speeches restating the law, covenant renewal, and the entry into the promised land.

Jewish tradition ascribes authorship to Moses, hence the Books of Moses, though modern scholarship attributes the texts to later editors and multiple sources known as the JEDP hypothesis. The Pentateuch is read cyclically in synagogues, with the yearly cycle completing on Simchat Torah.
